program: Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Wyoming
comments: I had a very disappointing experience applying to the PhD program in EECS at the University of Wyoming. I submitted my application in January and never received any clear communication regarding its completeness. There were no notifications about missing documents, and every time I reached out for a status update, I received vague or delayed responses. In several instances, there was no reply at all. The lack of professionalism from the department, including the Graduate Coordinator, was frustrating. As an applicant investing significant time, effort, and money into the process, I expected at least basic transparency and communication. Unfortunately, that standard was not met. What makes this worse is that the final rejection cited multiple concerns, but none of these were ever communicated earlier in the process, nor was there any opportunity to clarify or strengthen the application. It raises serious questions about how thoroughly applications are handled and whether they are reviewed in a timely and organized manner. Overall, the experience felt disorganized, dismissive, and disrespectful toward applicants. Based on this experience, I would strongly caution prospective students to think carefully before applying here. Applicants deserve timely communication, clear guidance, and professional treatment—none of which I experienced in this process.

Dear Applicant, Thank you for the time, effort, and passion you put into your application to the UCSC Physics graduate program. There is a person behind every application, statement of purpose, and letter of recommendation, and we truly appreciate the effort you contributed applying to our program. That is what makes it challenging to inform you we are unable to recommend you for admission for this coming fall. This was a difficult decision for our committee for two reasons: 1) this year’s applicant pool was exceptionally talented, and the level of research experience and academic dedication we saw was genuinely humbling; and 2) due to department funding and faculty research capacity we are simply unable to recommend offers of admission to all researchers we believe would thrive here. This decision is a reflection of our departmental constraints, not a reflection of your potential as a physicist. There are many paths towards scientific inquiry, and we hope you continue pursuing your interests in physics research. Understandably, many applicants ask us for feedback on their applications to see how they can improve in the future. Please understand due to the sheer number of requests we receive the committee is unable to provide comment on any individual's application. We trust that your continued efforts and dedication will open doors for you as you pursue your career. Thank you again for considering UC Santa Cruz. We wish you the very best in your next chapter.

All of us on the faculty here greatly admire your work and would be delighted to have you with us next year should a spot open. The truth is, determining “who gets in” versus “who gets waitlisted” once we have agreed on a group of writers we want to admit is always ridiculously difficult. This is an inexact business (and of course it’s not a “business” at all), and ours is a very small program by design. Please be aware that you are among a distinguished group of writers who received enthusiastic “yes” votes from every one of the relevant faculty. I can promise you that the very latest you will hear from us about your admission will be one week after April 15, which is the date by which all admitted students must either decline or accept our offer. It’s very possible that you will hear from us sooner, but I wouldn’t count on that, as many people wait until the last possible minute to say yes or no. All I can tell you for sure is that as soon as we know how many offers have been accepted, I will contact you one way or the other.
